  shrinks while depth grows) and place LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, and ResNet on the timeline. *(Understand)*

## Why This Matters

You would not rewrite a database engine to build a web app -- you import one. Computer vision works the
same way. The hard, expensive work of learning what edges, textures, and object-parts look like was
already done, once, on more than a million ImageNet photos, by networks the field spent a decade
refining. A **pretrained** network is that reusable engine, and **transfer learning** is the import
statement: freeze what it already knows, bolt a small new classifier on top, and learn your task from a
thousand examples instead of a few million.

Two ideas make this lesson. The first is **why** those very deep networks could be trained at all --
the **residual connection**, one small architectural trick. The second is **how** you reuse them. By
the end you will have taken a ResNet trained on ImageNet and, in about thirty seconds on a CPU, turned
it into a CIFAR-10 classifier that crushes a CNN trained from scratch on the same data.

## Two Datasets: ImageNet and CIFAR-10

Two datasets carry this lesson, and both are landmarks of the field.

**ImageNet** is a collection of photos -- about 14 million today -- sorted into about 22,000
categories. Jia Deng, Fei-Fei Li, and colleagues introduced it in 2009, and crowd workers on Amazon
Mechanical Turk checked the labels. Its best-known slice, used by the **ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC)**
from 2010 to 2017, has 1,000 classes and about 1.28 million training images. That yearly competition
was the field's scoreboard, scored by **top-5 error**: the share of test images whose true class is not
among the model's five best guesses. In 2012 AlexNet, a CNN, won it with a top-5 error of 15.3%, against 26.2%
for the runner-up, which used hand-designed features -- the result that started the deep-learning boom.
In 2015 ResNet brought the error down to 3.57%. ImageNet is free for non-commercial research but needs
a registration, which is why libraries ship the *weights* of models trained on it rather than the
images themselves. When this lesson calls a model "pretrained", it means trained on ILSVRC's 1,000
classes.

**CIFAR-10** is the small benchmark: 60,000 color images of 32x32 pixels in 10 classes, assembled by
Alex Krizhevsky, Vinod Nair, and Geoffrey Hinton and released in 2009. It is small enough to train on a
laptop, which made it the standard first test for new ideas; its sibling CIFAR-100 has 100 classes.
`torchvision.datasets` downloads it in one line, which is how the lab gets it.

| | ImageNet (the ILSVRC slice) | CIFAR-10 |
|---|---|---|
| Released | 2009 (Deng, Fei-Fei Li, et al.) | 2009 (Krizhevsky, Nair, Hinton) |
| Images | ~1.28 million train · 50,000 validation | 50,000 train · 10,000 test |
| Classes | 1,000 | 10 (6,000 images each) |
| Image size | varies; usually resized to 224x224 | 32x32, color |
| Role in this lesson | where the pretrained backbone learned its features | the small new task (the lab uses 100 images per class) |

Note the size gap in the last two rows. The lab enlarges each 32x32 CIFAR image to 96x96 so the
pretrained network has something closer to what it saw in training, which is why the lab's pictures look
blurry. Transfer has to bridge that gap: from sharp ImageNet photos to upscaled thumbnails.

Benchmark datasets have histories, too. CIFAR's images were drawn from **80 Million Tiny Images**, a
web-scraped collection whose creators withdrew it in 2020 after an audit found racist and misogynistic
labels (CIFAR was labeled separately, by hand, and remains in use). Around the same time, the ImageNet
team found that 1,593 of the 2,832 "person" categories in the full ImageNet (not the 1,000-class slice)
were potentially offensive and set out to remove them. A pretrained model carries whatever its training data contained, so find out what a model was
trained on before you build on it.

**Explore:** browse CIFAR-10 in the [Hugging Face dataset viewer](https://huggingface.co/datasets/uoft-cs/cifar10)
· the [CIFAR page](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~kriz/cifar.html) · [image-net.org](https://www.image-net.org/)
· the ILSVRC overview paper (Russakovsky et al.) on [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0575).

## The CNN Architecture Pattern

Real CNNs are built from the L18 pieces, stacked in a recurring rhythm: a few `Conv -> ReLU` layers,
then a **pooling** layer, then a few more `Conv -> ReLU`, then pool again, and so on. Two things happen
as you climb the stack. The image gets **smaller** in height and width (each pool halves it), and it
gets **deeper** -- later convolutional layers hold *more* feature maps. Shrinking the grid while
doubling the channels keeps the compute balanced and lets the network trade spatial detail for richer,
more abstract features. At the top sits a small fully connected **head** ending in logits, exactly as
in L18. A useful rule of thumb: prefer several small `3x3` kernels over one large kernel -- they see the
same region with fewer parameters.

That pattern has a history, and four names trace it -- the last three made their names in the ILSVRC
competition:

| Year | Network | What it added |
|---|---|---|
| 1998 | **LeNet-5** | the original conv/pool stack (tanh activations, average pooling) on handwritten digits |
| 2012 | **AlexNet** | bigger and deeper; **ReLU** and **dropout**; won ImageNet and started the deep-learning boom |
| 2014 | **VGG** | depth through uniform `3x3` convolutions -- simple and very deep |
| 2015 | **ResNet** | **residual connections**, which made 50-to-150-layer networks trainable |

## The Degradation Problem and Residual Connections

If depth helps, why not just keep stacking layers? Because past a point a **plain** deep network gets
*worse* -- and not from overfitting. Its **training** error goes up. A 56-layer plain net can train to a
higher error than a 20-layer one, even though the deeper net could in principle copy the shallower one
and add identity layers. The problem is **optimization**: gradients have to survive a long backward
journey (the L17 unstable-gradient story), and a deep stack of layers struggles to even learn to do
*nothing* where nothing is needed. This is the **degradation problem**.

ResNet's fix is almost embarrassingly simple. Instead of asking a block to compute a target mapping
`H(x)` directly, let it compute a **residual** `F(x)` and add the input back:

$$\text{output} = \operatorname{ReLU}\big(F(x) + x\big)$$

That `+ x` is the **skip** (or **shortcut**) **connection**. Now if the best thing a block can do is
nothing, it only has to drive `F(x)` toward zero -- an easy target -- and the **identity** passes
through untouched. Just as importantly, the skip gives gradients a direct path backward, so they reach
the early layers without being throttled. A **residual block** -- two convolutions plus a skip -- is
ResNet's repeating unit, and stacking them is what lets a 150-layer network train as easily as a
shallow one. Where L17's initialization and batch-norm *tamed* unstable gradients, residual connections
add a structural **highway** for them. (The same trick reappears in L22's Transformer blocks.) The lab
shows the degradation problem directly: a 19-layer CNN without skips never gets past guessing, while
the same network with skips trains normally.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  x["x (input)"] --> c1["Conv 3x3<br/>+ ReLU"]
  c1 --> c2["Conv 3x3"]
  x -- "skip (identity)" --> add(("+"))
  c2 --> add
  add --> r["ReLU"]
  r --> out["output"]
```

## Transfer Learning

Training a large network from scratch needs a large dataset and a lot of compute. Most of the time you
have neither -- and you do not need them, because someone already trained a network on a giant task.
**Transfer learning** reuses that work: take a model **pretrained** on a big dataset (typically
**ImageNet** -- 1.2 million images, 1000 classes) and adapt it to your smaller, related task.

The key is to split the network into two parts. The convolutional **backbone** learned *general* visual
features -- edges and textures in the low layers, object-parts higher up -- and those transfer well
across tasks. The final **head** (the classifier) is specific to the original 1000 classes and is
useless for yours. So you **replace the head** and choose how much of the backbone to reuse:

- **Feature extraction** -- **freeze** the entire backbone (`requires_grad = False`, so gradient descent
  leaves its weights fixed) and train *only* the new head. The backbone becomes a fixed function that
  turns each image into a vector of features; learning the head is fast and needs little data. This is
  the cheap, robust default.
- **Fine-tuning** -- after the head is trained, **unfreeze** the top block or two and continue training
  end-to-end at a **low** learning rate, so backprop gently adapts the high-level features without
  wrecking them. The more data you have, the more layers you can afford to unfreeze.

![Transfer learning with ResNet18, in three stages. Blue blocks hold weights learned on ImageNet, gray blocks are frozen copies, orange blocks are trained on the new task, and green bars are the 512 pooled features. Block sizes follow the shapes but are not to scale.](../assets/l19_transfer_learning.svg){#fig-transfer-learning fig-alt="Three rows of 3-D block diagrams of ResNet18. Row 1, pretrained on ImageNet: a 3 x 224 x 224 photo feeds blue blocks conv1 + pool and layer1 (64 x 56 x 56), layer2 (128 x 28 x 28), layer3 (256 x 14 x 14) and layer4 (512 x 7 x 7), then a pool bar of 512 features and a gray fc head for 1000 classes crossed out in red and labelled removed. An arrow labelled weights copied leads to row 2, feature extraction on CIFAR-10: a blurry 3 x 96 x 96 cat image feeds the same five blocks, now gray, with shapes 64 x 24 x 24 down to 512 x 3 x 3, under a brace labelled frozen backbone (requires_grad = False), then the 512 features and an orange new head, fc with 10 classes, trained. An arrow labelled then, if you have more data leads to row 3, fine-tuning: conv1 to layer3 stay gray under a brace labelled still frozen, layer4 is orange and labelled layer4 unfrozen, the head is orange, and a dashed arrow pointing back toward the input reads more data? unfreeze more blocks, from the top down (earliest layers last). A legend names the five colors."}

Read the figure row by row. **Row 1** is ResNet18 as it comes from ImageNet: its backbone shrinks a
224x224 photo to 512 numbers, and its head turns those into scores for 1,000 ImageNet classes -- useless
for a new task, so it is removed. **Row 2** is feature extraction, the lab's main recipe: the same
backbone, with every block frozen, now reads a 96x96 CIFAR image (the shapes are smaller, the weights are
the same), and only a new 10-class head is trained. **Row 3** is fine-tuning: the top block, `layer4`,
is unfrozen too and trained at a low learning rate. With more data you can unfreeze more blocks, working
down from the top; the earliest blocks, which detect edges and textures, are the last to unfreeze
because their features are the most general.

The guidelines are simple: freeze first and see how far it gets you; unfreeze top-down only if you need
more and have the data; reduce the learning rate when you unfreeze. Transfer learning works best with
deep **convolutional** networks (their low-level features are general) and when your inputs share
low-level structure with the originals -- which also means you must feed inputs at the expected size and
with the **same normalization** the model was trained with (ImageNet's per-channel mean and std).

In PyTorch the gateway is **`torchvision.models`**: a library of architectures with pretrained weights,
from AlexNet and VGG through ResNet, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, and Vision Transformers, loaded in one
line: `torchvision.models.resnet18(weights="DEFAULT")`. When you cannot get more labeled data, the other
cheap regularizer is **data augmentation** -- growing the training set with realistic variants (random
crops, horizontal flips, small rotations) applied on the fly each epoch. The lab ends with a short
measured taste of augmentation and other tricks.

## Where to Find Pretrained Models

`torchvision.models` is one of several places that publish pretrained weights. The main ones, and the
framework each serves:

| Hub | Framework | What you find there |
|-----------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| [torchvision.models](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/models.html) | PyTorch | the classic vision models: classification, detection, segmentation |
| [timm](https://huggingface.co/timm) | PyTorch | over a thousand image backbones; the widest catalog of CNNs and ViTs |
| [PyTorch Hub](https://pytorch.org/hub/) | PyTorch | research models published straight from their authors' repositories |
| [Keras Applications](https://keras.io/api/applications/) | TensorFlow / Keras | the classic ImageNet CNNs (ResNet, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, VGG, MobileNet) |
| [KerasHub](https://keras.io/keras_hub/) | Keras 3 (on a TensorFlow, JAX, or PyTorch backend) | vision and language models, with checkpoints hosted on Kaggle |
| [Kaggle Models](https://www.kaggle.com/models) | mostly TensorFlow / Keras, also PyTorch and JAX | the former TensorFlow Hub catalog (tfhub.dev links redirect here since 2023), plus Google and DeepMind models |
| [Hugging Face Hub](https://huggingface.co/models) | any (mostly PyTorch; each model card names its library) | the largest: vision, text, audio, and multimodal models |

: Where pretrained weights live, and which framework loads them {tbl-colwidths="[24,30,46]"}

Loading looks much the same everywhere -- one line, and several hubs build the "replace the head" step
into that line:

```python
# PyTorch
model = torchvision.models.resnet18(weights="DEFAULT")
model = torch.hub.load("pytorch/vision", "resnet18", weights="DEFAULT")
# timm: num_classes=10 swaps in a new 10-class head
model = timm.create_model("resnet50", pretrained=True, num_classes=10)
# Hugging Face transformers: num_labels=10 does the same
model = AutoModelForImageClassification.from_pretrained(
    "microsoft/resnet-50", num_labels=10, ignore_mismatched_sizes=True)

# Keras Applications: include_top=False drops the 1000-class head
model = keras.applications.ResNet50(weights="imagenet", include_top=False)
# KerasHub: num_classes=10 swaps in a new 10-class head
model = keras_hub.models.ImageClassifier.from_preset(
    "resnet_v2_50_imagenet", num_classes=10)
```

Two cautions. **Weights load only in the framework that saved them:** a PyTorch checkpoint needs PyTorch
and a Keras one needs Keras -- Keras 3 and KerasHub are the exception, since they run on any of the three
backends. On Hugging Face, filter by "Library" to see what you can load. **Weights come with a
license:** most are permissive, but not all (YOLO models from Ultralytics are AGPL, and the Llama family
has its own license), so check it before you build a product on one.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Forgetting to replace the head.** The pretrained head outputs the *original* number of classes
  (1000 for ImageNet). Swap in a new `Linear` with *your* number of classes.
- **Not freezing the backbone.** Leave millions of pretrained weights trainable on a few hundred images
  and they overfit instantly. Freeze first; that is the whole point.
- **Wrong input normalization.** A pretrained model expects its training-time preprocessing. Resize to
  the expected size and normalize with the **ImageNet** mean/std, or the features come out garbage.
- **Fine-tuning at a high learning rate.** A large step on unfrozen pretrained layers erases what they
  learned. Drop the learning rate when you unfreeze.
- **Assuming more layers always train better.** The degradation problem says otherwise -- that is exactly
  why residual connections had to be invented.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Freeze or fine-tune?"** -- Freeze first (feature extraction): it is fast, needs little data, and is
hard to get wrong. Fine-tune the top layers only if you have enough data and feature extraction is not
good enough -- and always drop the learning rate when you do.

**"Shouldn't the new head have a hidden layer, like 512 -> 256 -> 10?"** -- Many older tutorials do
that. They come from the VGG era, when the head sat on a flattened 7x7x512 feature map of 25,088 numbers
and VGG's own head had three dense layers. ResNet averages each feature map down to one number and uses
a single linear layer as its head, and a single linear layer on those 512 features is the standard
default today. A hidden layer can help with more data or images far from ImageNet; with little data it
mostly adds parameters. The lab's Exercise 2 measures it.

**"Which architecture should I pick?"** -- For most image tasks, start with a ResNet (e.g. `resnet18`
or `resnet50`); it is a reliable, well-supported default. Pick a smaller/faster model (MobileNet,
EfficientNet) for phones or tight latency, a larger one for maximum accuracy.

**"Why is ResNet everywhere?"** -- Residual connections made very deep networks trainable and turned out
to help almost any deep architecture. The idea -- add the input back around a block -- is now standard
far beyond vision, including in Transformers.

**"What about Vision Transformers?"** -- Attention-based models (L21, L22) now match or beat CNNs on
large datasets, and `torchvision.models` ships pretrained ViTs too. They are reused exactly the same
way: load pretrained, replace the head, freeze or fine-tune. Training any of these at scale, with GPUs
and full augmentation pipelines, is the CDAT 4013 lab's territory.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---|---|
| ImageNet / ILSVRC | ~1.28M photos, 1,000 classes; the competition (2010-2017) where modern CNNs proved themselves |
| CIFAR-10 | 60,000 tiny 32x32 images, 10 classes; the standard small benchmark |
| Architecture pattern | conv/ReLU + pool blocks: spatial size shrinks, depth (feature maps) grows; FC head on top |
| The timeline | LeNet (1998) -> AlexNet (2012) -> VGG (2014) -> ResNet (2015) |
| Degradation problem | very deep *plain* nets train *worse* -- an optimization failure, not overfitting |
| Residual / skip connection | `out = ReLU(F(x) + x)`; learn a residual, fall back to identity, shortcut for gradients |
| Transfer learning | reuse a model pretrained on a big task for a new, smaller, related one |
| Backbone + head | keep the general conv backbone; replace the task-specific classifier head |
| Feature extraction | freeze the backbone, train only the new head (cheap; little data) |
| Fine-tuning | unfreeze the top block(s), train end-to-end at a LOW learning rate |
| torchvision.models | one-line pretrained architectures: `resnet18(weights="DEFAULT")` |
| Model hubs | PyTorch: torchvision, timm, PyTorch Hub · Keras: Applications, KerasHub · both: Kaggle, Hugging Face |
